sources.entry: A Map of Sync categorizes state sync into 9 dimensions.

summary.title: A Map of Sync
summary.one_liner: A nine-dimension framework (data model, systems requirements, programming model) for comparing sync platforms like Linear, Dropbox, Figma, Replicache, Automerge, and Valorant.
takeaways: Sync platforms can be compared across nine dimensions: size, update rate, structure, input latency, offline support, concurrent clients, centralization, flexibility, and consistency.
Systems with high update rates tend to rely on in-memory structures, binary formats, and batching; low-rate systems often use slower, cheaper storage.
Offline support ranges from none (Valorant) to partial (Linear) to full (Obsidian, Dropbox), and it strongly shapes architecture.

CRDTs like Automerge resolve many conflicts automatically but generally offer weaker consistency guarantees, such as no cross-key invariants, while Replicache offers strong, transaction-based consistency through server authority.
summary.summary: The article from Convex's team proposes a taxonomy for state sync platforms, grouped into data model, systems requirements, and programming model categories with nine dimensions in total. Each dimension is explained with examples drawn from products such as Linear, Dropbox, Figma, Valorant, Replicache, and Automerge, and a comparison table rates each platform. The authors draw on their experience building sync at Dropbox and on Convex's ongoing work to extend its sync engine. The piece closes by promising a follow-up post on where Convex's sync engine falls on these dimensions.
